title: Spanish Plural Mistakes: Rules for -s, -es and More
seo_title: Spanish Plural Mistakes: Rules for -s, -es and More
meta_description: Spanish plural mistakes learners make: -s or -es, z to ces, accents that move, words that never change, gente and había, with clear fixes and a quiz.
excerpt: From lápices to la gente es: the plural slips I correct most, and how to fix them.

body_html:
Spanish plural mistakes look small, but they show up in almost every sentence. The basic rule is easy: add -s after a vowel and -es after a consonant. The problems come from the details: lápiz becomes lápices, canción loses its accent in canciones, joven gains one in jóvenes, some words never change, and a few words that are plural in English are singular in Spanish, like la gente. Here are the plural mistakes I correct most, with the fix for each.

Quick answer
  • Vowel + -s: casa → casas. Consonant + -es: árbol → árboles.
  • -z becomes -ces: vez → veces, luz → luces.
  • Accents can disappear or appear: canción → canciones, examen → exámenes.
  • La gente is singular: La gente es amable, never “la gente son”.
{{toc}}

Spanish plural mistakes: the basic rules

Word ends inRuleExamples
Unstressed vowelAdd -slibro → libros, mesa → mesas, calle → calles
ConsonantAdd -esciudad → ciudades, mujer → mujeres, papel → papeles
-zChange to -ceslápiz → lápices, nariz → narices, pez → peces
Stressed -í or -úUsually -es, -s also acceptedcolibrí → colibríes, menú → menús

The Real Academia Española sets out the full rules, including the exceptions, in its Diccionario panhispánico de dudas.

Accents that move

Adding a syllable can shift where the stress falls in writing, so the accent mark may disappear or appear. The pronunciation of the stressed syllable doesn’t change; only the spelling rule does.

  • Accent disappears: canción → canciones, francés → franceses, autobús → autobuses
  • Accent appears: joven → jóvenes, examen → exámenes, origen → orígenes
  • Stress moves (rare): carácter → caracteres, régimen → regímenes

If you want the full logic behind these marks, see {{link:spanish-accent-marks|Spanish accent marks}}.

{{image:2}}

Words that never change

Words that end in an unstressed vowel + -s or -x are the same in singular and plural. The article shows the number:

  • Days of the week: el lunes → los lunes, el viernes → los viernes
  • Words ending in -sis: la crisis → las crisis, el análisis → los análisis
  • Compound words: el paraguas → los paraguas, el abrelatas → los abrelatas
  • Others: el virus → los virus, el tórax → los tórax

So Los lunes voy al gimnasio means “On Mondays I go to the gym”. Writing “los luneses” is a classic beginner slip.

Gente, familia and other singular groups

This is the mistake I see most, even from advanced learners. In English, “people” takes a plural verb. In Spanish, la gente is grammatically singular:

  • La gente es muy amable aquí. People are very friendly here.
  • Mucha gente piensa que… A lot of people think that…

The same goes for la familia, el equipo and el público: Mi familia vive en Jalisco. If you want a plural, use las personas: Las personas que conocí son muy amables.

The opposite happens with a few words that are usually plural in Spanish: las vacaciones (vacation), los lentes (glasses, in Mexico), las tijeras (scissors).

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Hay and había never go plural

“There is” and “there are” are both hay in Spanish, and in the past both are había. Because the noun after them is the object, not the subject, the verb doesn’t become plural:

  • Hay muchos carros. There are a lot of cars.
  • Había muchas personas. There were a lot of people. (not “habían”)
  • Hubo dos accidentes. There were two accidents. (not “hubieron”)

Plural forms like “habían muchas personas” are common in everyday speech in many countries, but standard Spanish uses the singular, and it is what you should write. See {{link:tener-vs-haber|tener vs haber}} for more on this verb.

Agreement: the plural spreads

In Spanish, the plural doesn’t stop at the noun. Articles, adjectives and the verb all have to follow, and forgetting one of them is a very common slip:

  • Los carros rojo son caro. → Los carros rojos son caros.
  • Mis amiga mexicanas viene mañana. → Mis amigas mexicanas vienen mañana.

When you proofread, follow the noun through the sentence and check every word that describes it. This habit fixes plural and {{link:spanish-gender-mistakes|gender}} agreement at the same time.

{{image:3}}

Mixed groups, families and foreign words

  • Mixed groups use the masculine plural: mis hijos can mean my sons, or my sons and daughters. Los padres means parents, and los hermanos can mean siblings.
  • Family names don’t change: los García, los Pérez (the Garcías, the Pérezes).
  • Borrowed words: many add -s, as in los fans and los chats, while some add -es, as in los clubes. A dictionary is the safest guide.

Plural mistakes are one family among many in my guide to {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|common Spanish mistakes}}, alongside {{link:spanish-gender-mistakes|gender mistakes}} and {{link:spanish-article-mistakes|article mistakes}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Spanish plural mistakes are easy to fix once you know where to look: -z to -ces, accents that move, words that never change, and singular gente and había. Run through the quiz again next week, and check plurals whenever you proofread a message. For every other family of errors, see {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|common Spanish mistakes}}.

faq.q: How do you make nouns plural in Spanish?
faq.a: Add -s to words ending in an unstressed vowel and -es to words ending in a consonant. Words ending in -z change to -ces.
Singular: la gente es, la gente piensa. Use las personas if you need a plural.

faq.q: Why does canción lose its accent in the plural?
faq.a: Because the extra syllable changes which accent rule applies. The stress stays on the same syllable, but the mark is no longer needed.
It is common in speech, but standard Spanish uses the singular: había muchas personas.

questions.explain: The accent disappears when a syllable is added.
The accent appears in the plural.
Había stays singular in standard Spanish.
Days ending in -s don’t change in the plural.
